title: AI Assisted Research #5 — Can AI Help Us Discover New Physics? From Ideas to Equations
html:
One of the most fascinating aspects of physics is that the universe exhibits mathematical relationships that human beings can discover, describe, and use to make predictions.

We can calculate the motion of planets, predict the behavior of electromagnetic waves, and describe how gravity influences the passage of time.

But where did the equations that make these predictions possible come from?

Someone had to develop them.

This raises a question that has become increasingly important in our Beyond the Light Barrier research:

If physicists developed new mathematical descriptions of nature in the past, can we responsibly develop new equations today—and can artificial intelligence help us do it?

The answer is worth exploring, but it requires an important distinction.

Developing a new mathematical relationship is not the same as discovering a new physical law.

Mathematics allows us to describe many possible relationships. Nature determines which of those relationships accurately describe the physical universe.

Where Do Physics Equations Come From?

Scientific equations do not all originate in the same way.

Some emerge from careful observations. Others develop from mathematical reasoning, symmetry principles, or attempts to resolve contradictions between existing theories and experimental evidence.

Consider a few historical examples.

Newton and the Motion of Objects

Isaac Newton developed a mathematical framework connecting forces with changes in motion.

His second law is commonly expressed in modern notation as:

F = ma

Here, F represents net force, m represents mass, and a represents acceleration.

This familiar expression applies to an object of constant mass in an inertial reference frame. More generally, in Newtonian mechanics, net force is related to the rate of change of momentum.

Newton's original Principia, published in 1687, did not present the second law in the modern form F = ma. Its formulation described how an impressed force changes motion.

Newton's work built upon earlier mathematical developments and observations. Its importance came from the explanatory and predictive power of the resulting framework.

Maxwell and Electromagnetism

James Clerk Maxwell developed a unified mathematical description of electricity and magnetism.

His 1865 paper, A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field, developed a mathematical account of electromagnetic phenomena that included the propagation of electromagnetic disturbances.

The theory connected electromagnetic-wave propagation with the known speed of light.

This was an extraordinary connection: light could be understood as an electromagnetic phenomenon.

Maxwell's work illustrates how mathematical relationships can reveal implications that were not initially obvious from the observations used to develop them.

Einstein and Spacetime

Albert Einstein approached physics by examining fundamental assumptions about space, time, motion, and gravitation.

His 1905 special-relativity paper addressed the relationship between the laws of physics and measurements made by observers in relative inertial motion.

In 1915, Einstein completed the gravitational field equations of general relativity, relating spacetime geometry to energy and momentum.

The resulting theory provided testable predictions, including gravitational time dilation and the deflection of light.

In 1916, Einstein also investigated gravitational-wave solutions.

Nearly a century later, on September 14, 2015, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) directly detected gravitational waves from a binary black hole merger. The discovery was reported in a peer-reviewed paper published in February 2016.

This was not simply a mathematical calculation agreeing with another mathematical calculation. It was an experimental observation supporting a prediction of general relativity.

The historical lesson is not that any imaginative equation might be correct.

It is that questioning assumptions, developing mathematical descriptions, and testing their consequences can sometimes reveal a deeper understanding of nature.

When Existing Equations Are Not Enough

At Beyond the Light Barrier, we investigate advanced communication, propulsion, spacetime geometry, and related physical possibilities.

Many of our questions can be examined using established equations.

General relativity, electromagnetic theory, quantum mechanics, and classical mechanics already provide powerful mathematical tools.

We should use those tools wherever they are applicable.

However, we may encounter questions that existing models do not answer directly.

That does not necessarily mean existing physics is wrong.

Sometimes a known equation has not yet been applied to the particular configuration we want to study.

Sometimes the mathematical problem is difficult to solve.

Sometimes a model omits important physical effects.

And sometimes a question genuinely exposes an unresolved issue in our understanding of nature.

These possibilities must not be confused.

A gap in our current calculation is not automatically a gap in the laws of physics.

There is also an important distinction between developing a new equation and discovering a new physical law.

A new mathematical formulation may describe an approximation, a previously unexplored solution, or a more efficient way of representing established physics.

Such work can be valuable even when it introduces no new fundamental law.

Before proposing a new physical relationship, we should determine whether existing theory already describes the phenomenon.

If it does, we should investigate that relationship rather than inventing an unnecessary replacement.

If it does not, we may have a reason to explore a new mathematical model.

Can AI Help Develop New Mathematical Relationships?

Artificial intelligence can assist with mathematical exploration in several ways.

It can help identify assumptions, examine established equations, compare alternative formulations, perform symbolic manipulations, and develop computational tests.

It can also help us ask questions we might not otherwise have considered.

For example:

  • What happens if we change one assumption in an existing model?
  • Is there a mathematical relationship between two quantities that deserves investigation?
  • Could a proposed equation be derived from a more general principle?
  • Does a model behave correctly when a parameter approaches zero?
  • Does a proposed relationship contradict an established conservation law?

These questions are valuable because they transform an interesting idea into something we can investigate.

But AI introduces a particular danger.

A language model can produce an equation that looks mathematically sophisticated without establishing that it follows from valid physical assumptions.

It may combine familiar symbols in unfamiliar ways, omit a necessary term, or assume a relationship that has not been demonstrated.

It may also produce an expression that is mathematically consistent but physically meaningless.

This is why AI-generated equations must be treated as proposals requiring verification, not as discoveries.

The same principle applies when a proposed equation originates with a human researcher.

A Simple Example: Testing a Hypothetical Equation

Suppose we are exploring whether the response of a hypothetical physical system depends on a characteristic length, a characteristic time, and a dimensionless parameter describing some property of the system.

For illustration, define:

  • L — characteristic length, measured in meters.
  • T — characteristic time, measured in seconds.
  • q — dimensionless system parameter.
  • α — dimensionless coefficient.
  • v — proposed characteristic speed, measured in meters per second.

Assume L and T are positive.

We might propose:

v = (L/T)(1 + αq)

This equation is not a new law of physics or a BTLB research result. It is an invented mathematical example intended to demonstrate how a proposed relationship can be evaluated.

First Test: Are the Units Correct?

The quantity L/T has units of meters per second.

The factor (1 + αq) is dimensionless.

Therefore, the equation has the correct units for speed.

That is a necessary consistency check.

But it does not establish that the equation describes any real physical phenomenon.

We could construct infinitely many dimensionally consistent expressions that do not describe nature.

Second Test: Does It Have a Sensible Limiting Case?

Suppose q = 0.

The equation becomes:

v = L/T

This may be a useful reference limit if our assumptions define L/T as the baseline speed.

We could then investigate how the proposed response changes as q increases or decreases.

However, we would need a physical justification for the correction term αq.

Why should the correction be linear?

Why should it depend on q rather than q2?

Why should α be constant?

Why should the correction have that sign?

Dimensional consistency alone cannot answer these questions.

Third Test: Does It Produce Physically Meaningful Values?

We should also check whether the equation produces physically meaningful values across its intended range.

If v represents a nonnegative speed and L and T are positive, then the correction factor must satisfy:

1 + αq ≥ 0

If the expression becomes negative, the equation predicts a negative value for a quantity we defined as a speed.

That would require us to restrict the model's domain, revise the relationship, or reconsider the meaning of v.

If v instead represented a signed velocity component, a negative value might be entirely appropriate.

The interpretation of the mathematical variable matters.

Passing this check still would not establish that the equation describes nature.

Fourth Test: Does It Conflict With Established Physics?

Suppose someone interprets v as the speed at which information propagates through ordinary spacetime.

If the equation predicts a value greater than the speed of light in vacuum, we cannot conclude that faster-than-light communication is possible.

We would first need to determine whether v represents a local signal speed, a coordinate-dependent quantity, or something else entirely.

In established relativity, local causal propagation is constrained by the light-cone structure of spacetime.

Proposed global shortcuts or unusual spacetime geometries introduce additional questions about physical realizability, stability, and causality.

A mathematical expression that appears to predict superluminal motion does not resolve those questions.

Perhaps v does not represent a signal speed at all.

Perhaps the mathematical model describes an effective or coordinate-dependent quantity.

Perhaps the proposed relationship is simply incorrect.

These alternatives must be examined before interpreting the result.

Fifth Test: What Would Make the Equation Testable?

For a proposed relationship to become an empirically testable physical model, its mathematical quantities must ultimately connect to observable or independently constrained properties.

What physical system defines L and T?

How is q measured?

What determines α?

What observable outcome would distinguish this equation from existing models?

What measurement would contradict it?

Some theoretical investigations may remain valuable before a practical experiment is available.

They can reveal mathematical consequences, identify consistency conditions, or establish limits on possible physical behavior.

However, those achievements must not be confused with experimental confirmation.

If the relevant physical quantities cannot yet be operationally defined or constrained, the expression remains a mathematical proposal rather than an empirically validated model.

And that is an acceptable research outcome.

Not every idea must immediately become an experiment.

But its status must remain clear.

New Mathematics Does Not Automatically Mean New Physics

A proposed equation can pass several mathematical checks and still fail as a description of nature.

It may have correct units.

It may behave smoothly.

It may produce stable numerical solutions.

It may agree with a limited set of existing observations.

Yet it could still be physically incorrect.

For example, a model might violate an applicable conservation law, depend on an unjustified assumption, or fail when examined outside a narrow range of parameters.

A numerical simulation can reproduce the consequences of an incorrect equation with extraordinary precision.

The computer may solve the specified mathematical problem correctly while the underlying physical model is wrong.

This is one reason the Beyond the Light Barrier Research Method distinguishes analytic calculations, numerical results, independent reproduction, and physical experiments.

Each provides a different kind of evidence.

None should be represented as something it is not.

What This Means for Beyond the Light Barrier

Our research includes questions about wormhole communication, moving communication endpoints, advanced propulsion, and possible spacetime configurations.

These subjects require us to remain open to unfamiliar possibilities.

But openness does not mean assuming that a proposed mechanism is physically achievable.

Consider a hypothetical communication model.

We might develop equations describing signal propagation through a candidate spacetime geometry.

We could calculate travel times, frequency shifts, or the paths followed by light.

Such calculations might help determine whether the proposed geometry possesses mathematically interesting properties.

They would not, by themselves, establish that the geometry can exist in nature, be created, remain stable, or transmit information.

Likewise, an advanced propulsion model might describe a mathematical spacetime configuration with unusual travel-time properties.

We would still need to investigate its energy requirements, stress-energy conditions, stability, causality, and compatibility with established observations.

A new mathematical formulation might help us ask better questions.

It might reveal a contradiction.

It might show that a proposed approach is impossible under its assumptions.

Or it might identify a narrower question that can be investigated experimentally.

All of these outcomes have research value.

How We Would Evaluate a New BTLB Equation

If we develop a genuinely new mathematical relationship during our research, we should preserve its origin and evaluate it systematically.

The first requirement is to identify the physical question it is intended to answer.

We should then define its variables, units, assumptions, mathematical structure, and domain of applicability.

Next, we should determine whether it can be derived from established theory or whether it introduces a new physical hypothesis.

We should check dimensional consistency, limiting cases, symmetries, and relevant conservation laws.

Where possible, we should compare its predictions against existing experimental observations.

We should also examine whether alternative mathematical formulations produce distinguishable predictions.

If numerical simulations are necessary, their equations, parameters, initial and boundary conditions, numerical algorithms, and convergence behavior should be documented.

Independent reproduction should be evaluated from actual independence of methods and evidence—not merely from agreement between AI conversations.

Finally, we should identify what evidence would support the model and what evidence would falsify or constrain it.

If the model has no currently feasible experimental test, that limitation should be recorded rather than concealed.

A proposed equation that fails these checks should not simply disappear.

Its failure may reveal an invalid assumption or a constraint that helps guide future work.

Preserving that history is part of the scientific process.

Creativity and Scientific Discipline Belong Together

One concern about unconventional scientific research is that new ideas may be rejected simply because they are unfamiliar.

Another concern is that unconventional ideas may be accepted too readily because they are exciting.

Neither approach serves science well.

A new idea should be allowed to become a hypothesis.

A hypothesis should be allowed to become a mathematical model.

A mathematical model should be subjected to criticism and verification.

And the conclusions should follow the evidence, whether the outcome is encouraging, disappointing, or inconclusive.

AI can assist at each stage.

It can help generate alternatives, identify mathematical consequences, expose contradictions, and develop tests.

But AI cannot grant an idea physical validity merely by expressing confidence in it.

Neither can we.

Research Reflection

One of the things I find remarkable about physics is that human beings have developed mathematical descriptions capable of predicting phenomena far beyond ordinary experience.

That history encourages curiosity.

It suggests that we should not limit ourselves to asking only questions whose answers are already known.

At Beyond the Light Barrier, we want to remain willing to investigate new mathematical relationships when there is a scientifically defensible reason to do so.

We also want to remain willing to discover that our proposed relationships are wrong.

Both possibilities are part of research.

Artificial intelligence gives us an additional tool for exploring those possibilities, but it does not change the standard by which scientific claims must be judged.

Creativity allows us to imagine a relationship. Mathematics allows us to describe it precisely. Verification allows us to test its consequences. Evidence determines whether it describes nature.

Our goal is not to create equations that appear to prove faster-than-light communication or propulsion.

Our goal is to investigate what physics actually permits, identify what remains unknown, and develop testable explanations wherever possible.

That means being willing to explore new ideas.

It also means being willing to let those ideas fail.

And perhaps that is one of the most important lessons of AI-assisted research: the freedom to explore must be accompanied by the discipline to question what we find.

Sources and Further Reading

Historical Scientific Publications

  1. Newton, Isaac (1687). Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica. Foundational presentation of Newtonian mechanics and universal gravitation. For the historical distinction between Newton's original second-law formulation and modern F = ma notation, see the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Newton's Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica .
  2. Maxwell, James Clerk (1865). "A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field." Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 155, 459–512. DOI: 10.1098/rstl.1865.0008 .
  3. Einstein, Albert (1905). "Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper." Annalen der Physik, 17, 891–921 (series volume 322). DOI: 10.1002/andp.19053221004 .
  4. Einstein, Albert (1915). "Die Feldgleichungen der Gravitation." Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 844–847. Original publication .
  5. Abbott, B. P., et al. (LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration) (2016). "Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger." Physical Review Letters, 116, 061102. DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.116.061102 .

Beyond the Light Barrier Research Framework

  1. Beyond the Light Barrier Research Method v1.2. Evidence classification, verification, falsification, and preservation of negative results.
  2. BTLB Software Development Standards v1.1. AI-assisted software development, validation, and limitations of AI-based reproduction claims.
  3. Beyond the Light Barrier Research State v1.11. Research status, model limitations, and evidence classifications.
  4. AI Assisted Research #4 — Collaboration, Verification, and Accountability. Previous article in this series.

Evidence classification: This article is an educational and methodological discussion drawing on established physical theory, historical scientific developments, and BTLB research principles. Its mathematical example is explicitly hypothetical and has not been calibrated against a physical system. It does not introduce a validated BTLB physical model, report a new numerical research result, establish independent reproduction, or describe a new physical experiment.

    Or it might identify a narrower question that can be investigated
    experimentally.
  

  
All of these outcomes have research value.

  
How We Would Evaluate a New BTLB Equation

  

    If we develop a genuinely new mathematical relationship during our research,
    we should preserve its origin and evaluate it systematically.
  

  

    The first requirement is to identify the physical question it is intended to
    answer.
  

  

    We should then define its variables, units, assumptions, mathematical
    structure, and domain of applicability.
  

  

    Next, we should determine whether it can be derived from established theory
    or whether it introduces a new physical hypothesis.
  

  

    We should check dimensional consistency, limiting cases, symmetries, and
    relevant conservation laws.
  

  

    Where possible, we should compare its predictions against existing
    experimental observations.
  

  

    We should also examine whether alternative mathematical formulations produce
    distinguishable predictions.
  

  

    If numerical simulations are necessary, their equations, parameters, initial
    and boundary conditions, numerical algorithms, and convergence behavior
    should be documented.
  

  

    Independent reproduction should be evaluated from actual independence of
    methods and evidence—not merely from agreement between AI conversations.
  

  

    Finally, we should identify what evidence would support the model and what
    evidence would falsify or constrain it.
  

  

    If the model has no currently feasible experimental test, that limitation
    should be recorded rather than concealed.
  

  

    A proposed equation that fails these checks should not simply disappear.
  

  

    Its failure may reveal an invalid assumption or a constraint that helps
    guide future work.
  

  
Preserving that history is part of the scientific process.

  
Creativity and Scientific Discipline Belong Together

  

    One concern about unconventional scientific research is that new ideas may
    be rejected simply because they are unfamiliar.
  

  

    Another concern is that unconventional ideas may be accepted too readily
    because they are exciting.
  

  
Neither approach serves science well.

  
A new idea should be allowed to become a hypothesis.

  
A hypothesis should be allowed to become a mathematical model.

  
A mathematical model should be subjected to criticism and verification.

  

    And the conclusions should follow the evidence, whether the outcome is
    encouraging, disappointing, or inconclusive.
  

  
AI can assist at each stage.

  

    It can help generate alternatives, identify mathematical consequences,
    expose contradictions, and develop tests.
  

  

    But AI cannot grant an idea physical validity merely by expressing
    confidence in it.
  

  
Neither can we.

  
Research Reflection

  

    One of the things I find remarkable about physics is that human beings have
    developed mathematical descriptions capable of predicting phenomena far
    beyond ordinary experience.
  

  
That history encourages curiosity.

  

    It suggests that we should not limit ourselves to asking only questions
    whose answers are already known.
  

  

    At Beyond the Light Barrier, we want to remain willing to investigate new
    mathematical relationships when there is a scientifically defensible reason
    to do so.
  

  

    We also want to remain willing to discover that our proposed relationships
    are wrong.
  

  
Both possibilities are part of research.

  

    Artificial intelligence gives us an additional tool for exploring those
    possibilities, but it does not change the standard by which scientific
    claims must be judged.
  

  

    

      
        Creativity allows us to imagine a relationship. Mathematics allows us to
        describe it precisely. Verification allows us to test its consequences.
        Evidence determines whether it describes nature.
      
    

  

  

    Our goal is not to create equations that appear to prove faster-than-light
    communication or propulsion.
  

  

    Our goal is to investigate what physics actually permits, identify what
    remains unknown, and develop testable explanations wherever possible.
  

  
That means being willing to explore new ideas.

  
It also means being willing to let those ideas fail.

  

    And perhaps that is one of the most important lessons of AI-assisted
    research: the freedom to explore must be accompanied by the discipline to
    question what we find.
